title: Sistem Pakar Diagnosa Penyakit Tanaman Cabai dan Tomat Menggunakan Metode Forward Chaining di Desa Negeri Agung Selagai Lingga Lampung Tengah Berbasis Android
abstract: Sistem pakar bertujuan untuk memasukkan pengetahuan manusia ke dalam komputer sehingga komputer dapat menyelesaikan masalah seperti yang biasa dilakukan oleh para ahli. Dengan menggunakan sistem pakar ini, orang awam juga dapat menyelesaikan masalah yang cukup rumit yang sebelumnya hanya dapat diselesaikan oleh para ahli. Sistem pakar, yang dirancang dan diimplementasikan dengan bantuan bahasa pemrograman tertentu, dapat membantu para ahli menyelesaikan masalah dengan cara yang sama seperti yang dilakukan oleh para ahli atau pakar. Forward chaining memanfaatkan penalaran maju sehingga sistem pakar dapat mendiagnosa penyakit berdasarkan input gejala user. Ini memudahkan konsultasi karena pertanyaan gejala yang diajukan hanya berkaitan dengan penyakit yang dialami. Seperti dalam peningkatan hasil cabai dan tomat tentu tidak terlepas dari produktivitas yang baik, peningkatan akan menurun jika banyak tanaman cabai dan tomat yang terserang penyakit. Selama ini, masyarakat atau orang awam hanya melihat penyakit tanaman cabai dan tomat tanpa mengetahui gejalanya. Untuk mengatasi hal ini, diperlukan ahli yang memahami penyakit cabai dan tomat. Aplikasi Sistem Pakar berbasis Android akan dibuat untuk menyelesaikan masalah ini. Sistem Pakar akan digunakan di semua bidang, salah satunya di bidang hortikultura. Salah satu manfaat sistem pakar dalam tanaman hortikultura adalah memudahkan petani menemukan penyakit pada cabai dan tomat, sehingga petani dapat mengetahui jenis penyakit dan cara penanganannya secara cepat tanpa harus menunggu tenaga ahli yang memiliki kompetensi di bidang itu.

title: State, Action, and Transition: An Application-Oriented Bottleneck-Driven Survey of World Models
abstract: World models represent environments and predict how their states evolve under interventions. Their use in generative simulation and interactive environments, autonomous driving, and robotics and embodied control is growing, yet application validation remains fragmented across model families. Using the relation st+1∼pθ(⋅∣st,at), this review organizes the field around state representation, action representation, and transition modeling. We compare visual and geometric states with object-centric or belief/latent organization; semantic, hierarchical, latent, and executable actions; and autoregressive, diffusion-based, predictive latent, explicit-simulation, and learned–physics hybrid transitions. Across the three applications, we connect these choices to identity drift, non-executable plans, unsafe multimodal forecasts, long-horizon instability, and sim-to-real degradation. We then link each failure to six diagnostic dimensions: perceptual fidelity, physical validity, action consistency, rollout stability, calibration, and decision utility. The synthesis provides a cross-application engineering matrix and motivates Active Intervention Loops, Physical Laws Internalization, and Progressive Structural Integration. It identifies the State–Action–Transition commitments that shape application suitability and separates visual plausibility from evidence of interactive or deployment readiness.

title: Meta-Component Selection Method of Mission Software Based on NSGA-II
abstract: For UAV swarm–based disaster response scenarios involving collaborative area search, identification of high-priority targets, and target information transmission, existing foundational components can partially reuse capabilities from emergency command-and-control (C2) software. However, software capability requirements in dynamic environments are difficult to enumerate exhaustively in advance, while the provisioning and updating of reusable components remain insufficiently efficient. Consequently, current approaches struggle to satisfy the stringent real-time requirements for agile, on-demand software generation at the frontline. On this basis, this paper proposes a multi-objective meta-component selection method of UAV swarms based on Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). A meta-component description model covering functional coverage, interface constraints, dependency and mutual exclusion relationships, runtime, memory footprint, energy overhead, reliability and security level is constructed. The meta-component selection problem is transformed into a constrained multi-objective combinatorial optimization problem. Fast non-dominated sorting, crowding distance maintenance and constraint repair strategies are adopted to solve the Pareto-optimal component set, and a multi-index comprehensive evaluation method is utilized to select a compromise scheme from the Pareto set. Simulation experiments are carried out with eight types of tactical software functions and 32 candidate meta-components under fixed random seeds and reproducible experimental parameters. The results show that the Monte Carlo estimation yields an HV ratio of 0.998 and an ϵ-coverage of 1.000; the TOPSIS compromise solution requires 306.3 ms of runtime, 601.9 MB of memory, and 6.511 J·min−1 of energy consumption.

A meta-component description model covering functional coverage, interface constraints, dependency and mutual exclusion relationships, runtime, memory footprint, energy overhead, reliability and security level is constructed. The meta-component selection problem is transformed into a constrained multi-objective combinatorial optimization problem. Fast non-dominated sorting, crowding distance maintenance and constraint repair strategies are adopted to solve the Pareto-optimal component set, and a multi-index comprehensive evaluation method is utilized to select a compromise scheme from the Pareto set. Simulation experiments are carried out with eight types of tactical software functions and 32 candidate meta-components under fixed random seeds and reproducible experimental parameters. The results show that the Monte Carlo estimation yields an HV ratio of 0.998 and an ϵ-coverage of 1.000; the TOPSIS compromise solution requires 306.3 ms of runtime, 601.9 MB of memory, and 6.511 J·min−1 of energy consumption.

title: Optimising multipartite entanglement manipulation in quantum networks
abstract: Long-range, genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) between distant parties in a quantum network is a crucial resource for distributed quantum information processing. Through controlled manipulation of short-range GME states in the network via stochastic local operations aided by classical communication (SLOCC), long-range GME can be established between selected target nodes on demand. Optimizing such multipartite entanglement distribution protocols under constraints imposed by the network architecture, target-node set, and available resource budget is a key challenge in resource-efficient manipulation of GME. We present a general operational framework for manipulating GME in quantum networks by classifying the relevant networking operations into three broad primitives-inflation, deflation, and purification-reflecting their effect on the proliferation of GME through general bounds and illustrative examples. We show how these primitives can be combined to construct a broad class of multipartite quantum repeater protocols, enabling their systematic optimization, and demonstrate the framework with a simple example. Applying our approach to networks of Dür-Cirac-Tarrach states reveals a rich landscape of achievable end-to-end GME and accessible entanglement classes. More generally, our framework provides a systematic approach to the construction and optimization of multipartite quantum repeater protocols for scalable and resource-efficient GME distribution in quantum networks.

title: First Mathematical Runtime Analyses of Evolutionary Multitask Multi-Objective Optimization
abstract: To facilitate the solving of complex problems, evolutionary multitask optimization is regarded as a promising technique due to its capacity for cross-task knowledge transfer. In contrast to empirical evidences, no mathematical runtime support exists for this technique within the domain of multi-objective optimization. In this work, we aim to fill this important gap. We analyze how the representative multiobjective multifactorial evolutionary algorithm (MO-MFEA) covers the Pareto fronts of two bi-objective problems simultaneously. For the two-task problem of maximizing the classic bi-objective OMM and the multimodal OJZJ benchmarks, the MO-MFEA requires only an expected runtime of $O(n^2 \log n)$---the same as optimizing the simple OMM alone---yet achieves a speedup by a factor of $Θ(n^{k-1}/\log n)$ compared to optimizing OJZJ alone (with gap size $k$). Similarly, for the task pair comprising the classic LOTZ and the multimodal DLTB benchmarks, a speedup of $Θ(n)$ is attained over optimizing DLTB alone, while the runtime matches that of optimizing LOTZ alone.

title: Reaction Attack on CKKS Deployments with Asymptotically Optimal Query Complexity
abstract: We study a protocol-level reaction leakage in CKKS deployments where public coefficient-to-slot (C2S) evaluation keys are combined with a client's 1-bit validity response. Under this deployment surface, a malicious evaluator can recover a ternary secret key using asymptotically optimal $O(H)$ reaction queries, where $H$ is the entropy of the secret key. The attack does not break RLWE or CKKS IND-CPA security. Instead, it exploits the interaction between client-side validity reactions and public homomorphic linear transformations. A shift of a public encryption key yields a ciphertext whose plaintext is a function of the secret key; the public ${\sf C2S}$ layer then repacks this information to construct a ciphertext whose validity depends strictly on whether a targeted secret coefficient matches a guessed value. Furthermore, each submitted query is independently randomized with a fresh encryption of zero, so that each resulting malicious ciphertext appears entirely distinct, thereby allowing the attack to simply evade trivial detection mechanisms on the client side. We implemented the full end-to-end attack in Lattigo v6.2.0 and recovered the full secret key across four parameter sets drawn from standard CKKS presets. For uniform ternary secrets, the attack uses $O(N)$ queries and is within a factor $2/\log_2 3 < 2$ of the oracle-only entropy lower bound. For sparse ternary secrets, a tailored variant further reduces the number of queries in practice. Our results show that observable validity reactions form a practical key-recovery channel in CKKS deployments exposing this surface, even when the underlying cryptographic assumptions remain intact.

title: Adaptive Randomized Neural Networks for PDEs: Structure-Aware Feature Redistribution and Residual-Driven Block Enrichment
abstract: Randomized neural networks retain an output-linear least-squares solve, but globally sampled random features may fail to capture the spatial and scale structure of PDE solutions. We propose SFRBE--RaNN, a two-stage adaptive trial-space construction. SFR redistributes a fixed feature budget according to regional indicator masses and adapts regional weight scales through low-dimensional residual-based optimization. RBE constructs nonredundant enrichments by screening multiple activation families, removing represented response directions, and selecting the smallest admissible prefix. For solution-dependent operators, candidates are screened with a frozen operator and accepted only after nonlinear residual verification. For fixed linear problems, we establish an exact discrete residual-reduction identity and a conditional solution-error estimate. Building on this identity, we combine safeguarded SFR with RBE capture factors to derive a finite-horizon error bound involving baseline best approximation and empirical consistency, together with a conditional random-search success-probability bound. Numerical experiments on localized, multiscale, and nonlinear space--time problems demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

title: Classical methods for modern applications: synthetic tabular data generation using lightweight discrete response continuous latent variable model
abstract: In this paper, we present a lightweight algorithm for modelling tabular data containing both continuous and discrete variables. The method uses empirical marginal distributions and a selected quantile function to transform the data into a continuous latent space, where a distribution of choice, e.g. a multivariate Gaussian, can be efficiently estimated and applied. While this approach is closely related to classical well-established machine learning methods, we present a novel adaptation that fits well within the contemporary computational ecosystem. Unlike in the case of deep architectures, it results in a simple implementation with few dependencies, robust training/estimation, as well as efficient sampling. The transformation preserves complex marginal distributions and correlations, providing high-fidelity models, especially for data with unimodal distributions. One of the key characteristics of the proposed approach is its continuous representation of discrete variables. While highly desirable, this introduces a significant challenge, since a single observation corresponds to a region rather than a point in the latent space. We show that this ambiguity naturally leads to a Monte Carlo expectation-maximisation (MCEM) formulation, whose auxiliary objective can be expressed as a weighted latent-space likelihood. This, in turn, allows conventional maximum-likelihood estimators to be used within an efficient and robust optimisation procedure.

title: Dynamic ordering in sequence generation in Transformers: experiments on low-resource Tagging scenarios
abstract: This paper introduces TagInsert, a Transformer-based model that challenges the common left-to-right (L2R) generation paradigm in Transformers, for sequence labelling tasks where dependencies may not naturally align with a L2R order. TagInsert lifts the L2R constraint by removing the decoder-side attention mask and enabling the model to decide a preferred order of tag generation at inference time. We experiment on the common Part-of-Speech tagging and the more complex Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) supertagging tasks on multiple languages and low-resource data settings. We show that, although encoder-only models like BERT remain strong performers for tagging tasks, TagInsert frequently outperforms a L2R encoder-decoder model, achieves results comparable to encoder-only models under data-scarce conditions, and shows better results on the long-tail of rare categories. Our analyses show that TagInsert alleviates error propagation typical of autoregressive models by learning to defer difficult predictions to later stages in the decoding process.

title: Rethinking the Role of Tool Graph Memory in Multi-Turn Tool Use
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents solve complex tasks by calling external tools over multiple turns. Recent work has proposed tool graph memory, which stores past experience as tool transitions to guide subsequent selection. However, it remains unclear whether this component consistently improves agents' tool use or undermines it. We evaluate tool graph memory on nine models and two benchmarks, finding that it seldom improves significantly over baselines, and that its gains, where present, cost over twice the LLM calls. The memory's guidance is often incorrect, and random or no guidance retains most of the gain, implying that the benefit stems from extra computation rather than the memory itself. Moreover, even with the correct next tool suggested, many failures remain, such as giving up without a tool call. Storing the same experience instead as textual insights outperforms tool graph memory with almost no extra LLM calls. This suggests that memory serves better as a soft prior than as a prescription of the next tool, leading to a more effective and generalizable solution.

title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards
abstract: Reward learning typically assumes the human's input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features---or aspects of the task---better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot. Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn't know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human's attention on exactly those features. In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to $30.8\%$ in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.

title: Towards Continual Learning: Mitigating Forgetting With Subspace Tuning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire new skills through fine-tuning, but it can destroy capabilities they already have: catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle to continual learning in LLMs. Recent works connect forgetting to how far, and along which directions, fine-tuning moves the weights. On-policy methods such as reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation avoid updating the principal singular directions of weight matrices and thus forget less. In contrast, SFT concentrates updates along these directions and is susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. In this work, we introduce Subspace Tuning (SST), which restricts each weight update to the bottom singular subspace, eliminating changes along the principal directions. SST is optimizer-agnostic and composes well with fine-tuning recipes including SFT and self-distillation. SST combines tight subspace protection, dense gradient estimation, and a simple refresh mechanism, enabling stronger learning than prior orthogonal fine-tuning methods. With these mechanisms, protecting as much as 99\% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention while preserving strong target-task performance. This behavior strengthens with model and data size and nearly eliminates forgetting in the large-model regime. SST also keeps the model close to its base distribution, inducing $2$--$4\times$ less KL drift than the baseline recipes. Overall, SST advances the learning--forgetting Pareto frontier, making it a practical default for fine-tuning pre-trained language models.

title: MARS: A Momentum-Aware Adaptive Rating System for Personalized Assessment
abstract: Adaptive assessment systems personalize learning by estimating learner proficiency and recommending suitable questions. However, many existing approaches rely on fixed difficulty labels, static rating updates, or black-box prediction models that provide limited control over rating stability, interpretability, and time-constrained routing. This paper proposes MARS, a Momentum-Aware Adaptive Rating System for interpretable adaptive assessment. MARS represents the question bank as a directed weighted knowledge graph and updates learner proficiency using dynamic rating sensitivity, response quality, and momentum-aware learner velocity. We also formulate a time-budgeted mark-maximization objective in which the policy selects questions within a fixed test duration under negative marking. Experiments on ASSISTments 2009 and MARS-SimExam evaluate MARS for prediction, rating stability, and adaptive routing. Results show that MARS provides smoother rating updates than Fixed Elo and achieves the highest score under time-budgeted negative-marking routing, improving the total score by 8.09 over the strongest baseline and reducing overtime violations from 50% to 5.6%. These results suggest that MARS is suitable for real-time, interpretable, and deployment-friendly adaptive assessment.

title: Da sintaxe ao discurso: Evidências introdutórias da correlação entre Universal Dependencies e Rhetorical Structure Theory
abstract: A identificação automática de relações discursivas constitui um desafio central no Processamento de Línguas Naturais, especialmente para o português brasileiro, devido à escassez de recursos anotados e à variabilidade dos mecanismos de sinalização discursiva. Neste trabalho introdutório investigamos a correlação entre relações discursivas da Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) e relações de dependência sintática do modelo Universal Dependencies (UD) em textos jornalísticos. Analisamos cinco relações RST frequentes no gênero, combinando análises quantitativas e qualitativas. Os resultados indicam que cada relação discursiva apresenta características sintático-discursivas distintas.

evidence.title: Da sintaxe ao discurso: Evidências introdutórias da correlação entre Universal Dependencies e Rhetorical Structure Theory
evidence.abstract: A identificação automática de relações discursivas constitui um desafio central no Processamento de Línguas Naturais, especialmente para o português brasileiro, devido à escassez de recursos anotados e à variabilidade dos mecanismos de sinalização discursiva. Neste trabalho introdutório investigamos a correlação entre relações discursivas da Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) e relações de dependência sintática do modelo Universal Dependencies (UD) em textos jornalísticos. Analisamos cinco relações RST frequentes no gênero, combinando análises quantitativas e qualitativas. Os resultados indicam que cada relação discursiva apresenta características sintático-discursivas distintas.

title: EL-RAKHAWI FAULT-TOLERANT QUANTUM COMPUTING ARCHITECTURE: NEUROMORPHIC TOPOLOGICAL ERROR CORRECTION AND DYNAMIC ENVIRONMENTAL DECOUPLING FOR SCALABLE, COMMERCIAL-GRADE QUANTUM SUPREMACY
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) Architecture revolutionizes quantum computing by solving the critical decoherence and overhead bottleneck that has prevented commercial-grade quantum supremacy. Addressing the fragility of qubits and the prohibitive 1000:1 physical-to-logical qubit ratio of traditional Quantum Error Correction, FTQC integrates four novel modules: a Topologically Protected Logical Qubit Substrate encoding information non-locally using non-Abelian anyons for passive immunity against local noise; a Neuromorphic Quantum Error Correction (N-QEC) Engine employing ultra-low-power analog neuromorphic hardware for real-time syndrome decoding with sub-microsecond latency, learning non-Markovian noise profiles; a Dynamic Environmental Decoupling Matrix using predictive machine learning to proactively cancel environmental perturbations before decoherence occurs; and a Noise-Aware Quantum Compiler optimizing circuit routing to minimize depth and error probability. Performance is quantified by the El-Rakhawi Quantum Fault-Tolerance Efficiency Metric (EQFTEM), yielding Logical Operations per Joule, directly linking computational throughput to thermodynamic cost. This architecture reduces the overhead ratio to <100:1, making million-qubit fault-tolerant machines commercially viable, unlocking precise simulation of complex quantum systems, post-quantum cryptography, and global optimization, while democratizing quantum access through reduced energy requirements.

abstract: Supplementary material (ESM 1) for the manuscript “Lifetime quantum cost of quantum-kernel support vector machines for IoT classification: a pre-registered simulation study”. title: Robust Autonomous Lunar Landing Under Uncertain Physics
abstract: The project studies whether training an agent across randomized environment physics can improve its performance on previously unseen conditions compared with training under fixed physics. It uses the LunarLander-v3 environment and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), alongside a custom PyTorch actor–critic implementation and controlled evaluation experiments. The research focuses on two questions: Does training across randomized physical conditions improve generalization to previously unseen environment conditions compared with fixed-condition training? How does robustness vary across different training configurations and evaluation scenarios? The repository contains experimental implementations, training and evaluation scripts, model artifacts where included, and supporting results intended to make the research process easier to inspect and reproduce. The experimental workflow includes comparisons between agents trained under fixed and randomized physics, evaluation across multiple physical scenarios and random seeds, and investigation of the limitations of different training approaches. A standalone actor–critic implementation is also included as an implementation experiment. This release is intended to support transparent experimentation, reproducibility, and further research into robust reinforcement learning for autonomous landing tasks. Repository: https://github.com/empowered-aerial/LunarWing

title: EmoTweetJawa: A Dataset of Javanese Tweets for Sentiment Classification
abstract: EmoTweetJawa is a dataset of Javanese-language tweets for sentiment classification (Positive/Negative/Neutral), collected from Twitter/X using Javanese hashtags (#quotesjowo, #jowobaperan, #bosojowo, etc.). The dataset contains three files: (1) EmoTweetJawa-Corpus.csv, the raw unlabeled tweet corpus (text and engagement metadata); (2) EmoTweetJawa-Annotations.csv, individual sentiment labels from three independent human annotators per tweet; and (3) EmoTweetJawa-GroundTruth.csv, the final ground-truth label for each tweet, resolved by majority vote across the three annotators with manual reconciliation of disagreements. This dataset supports research on sentiment analysis and NLP for Javanese, a low-resource regional language of Indonesia.

title: Adaptive Self–Mutual Distillation in World Models: A Unified Framework for State-Dependent Knowledge Transfer and Cooperative Model Evolution
abstract: World models provide internal representations of environmental states, dynamics, and possible future outcomes, enabling systems to reason about actions before interacting with the external environment. However, the mechanisms through which world models improve their internal representations remain an important research problem. Self-distillation can reinforce a model's own knowledge, whereas mutual distillation can transfer complementary knowledge between interacting models. Using either mechanism exclusively may be suboptimal when model confidence, knowledge quality, environmental conditions, and computational resources vary over time. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Mutual Distillation in World Models (ASMD-WM), a conceptual framework that integrates self-models, mutual models, and world models into a unified architecture. The framework dynamically selects between self-distillation, mutual distillation, and a hybrid mode according to the estimated utility of each learning mechanism. Self-distillation consolidates internally generated knowledge, mutual distillation transfers complementary information between model components, and world-model consistency provides an additional constraint on whether transferred knowledge improves environmental prediction. A state-dependent controller considers predictive uncertainty, disagreement, expected knowledge gain, computational cost, and temporal consistency to determine the appropriate distillation strategy. The framework also incorporates reliability-aware transfer weights, safeguards against negative knowledge transfer, and a mechanism for retaining previously useful knowledge. The proposed framework differs conceptually from conventional fixed-direction teacher–student distillation, static mutual distillation, and world-model self-distillation by treating the choice between self-directed and reciprocal knowledge transfer as an explicit decision problem within a world-model architecture. This paper formalizes the architecture, objective functions, adaptive switching mechanism, learning algorithm, evaluation protocol, and research hypotheses. It does not claim experimentally validated improvements. Instead, it establishes a testable foundation for investigating whether adaptive switching between self-distillation and mutual distillation can improve predictive accuracy, knowledge retention, sample efficiency, and computational efficiency in non-language-model world-model systems.

title: Predicting pathogen-positive blood culture episodes at two hours using electronic health record data
abstract: Most blood cultures obtained early in hospitalization do not yield a pathogen. We evaluated prediction 2 h after the first blood-culture record using MIMIC-IV. Adults with an initial routine culture record within 24 h of hospital presentation were eligible if alive and still receiving care at prediction. The cohort included 145,914 encounters, 99.3% eventually admitted, and 6,404 pathogen-positive episodes (4.39%). Comparisons at 2, 4 and 6 h supported the earliest tested prediction time because later gains were small and uncertain. The primary XGBoost model was evaluated in 11,523 test encounters; 242 episodes were positive (2.10%). AUROC was 0.819 (95% CI 0.792–0.844), average precision 0.124 (0.096–0.167), and Brier score 0.0201. The top 5% of predicted risk contained 81 positives among 577 encounters, giving 14.0% positivity and 6.68-fold enrichment. Laboratory values, particularly lymphocyte percentage, contributed most to prediction. Secondary analyses assessed the added value of previous culture results. Mean predicted risk was 3.78%, compared with 2.10% observed. This 2-h model was able to concentrate pathogen-positive episodes in higher-risk groups, but calibration and transportability require further validation before clinical use.

title: Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamics for Efficient Image Generation
abstract: Token merging has emerged as an effective training-free strategy for accelerating diffusion models by reducing redundant token computation while minimizing generation degradation. A key challenge is determining which tokens can be safely merged and which should be preserved for subsequent computation. Existing method addresses this by preserving prompt-aligned foreground regions, thereby protecting semantically relevant structures. However, this text-relevance criterion overlooks background objects, local details that are not explicitly mentioned in the prompt, leading to degraded structural coherence. In this work, we propose Dynamics-aware Token Merging (DaTMe), a training-free framework that grounds token merging in the underlying diffusion dynamics. Our key insight is that token importance should reflect whether a token remains unresolved during denoising and whether it carries structural information. To this end, DaTMe constructs a dynamics- aware importance map from the Tweedie denoised estimate. The map combines a temporal signal, measuring inter-step changes in the predicted clean image, with a structural signal, capturing local high-frequency content such as boundaries and fine details. Using this map, DaTMe adaptively assigns tokens into merging roles under a given compression ratio: important tokens are preserved as anchors, while tokens that are both temporally stabilized and structurally homogeneous are selected as safe merge candidates. Experiments on PixArt-a and FLUX demonstrate that DaTMe maintains visual fidelity across the entire image, highlighting diffusion dynamics as an effective token-level merging decision in efficient generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/SeungJuCha/DaTMe.

title: Reinforcement Learning-driven Diffusion Models: Language, Vision, and Beyond
abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have steadily demonstrated outstanding performance in high-fidelity, controllable generation across diverse scenarios, following the "pretraining-finetuning" paradigm established in LLMs. Despite these advances, conventional DMs still face critical limitations in sophisticated reasoning, autonomous exploration of generation pathways, and adaptability to complex, human-aligned objectives. Inspired by RLHF's success in LLMs, RL has recently emerged as a pivotal post-training mechanism to iteratively refine DMs through reward-driven trajectory optimization. This paper presents the first comprehensive review of RL-driven DMs and an empirical analysis of how RL reshapes the diffusion process towards experience-centric, goal-directed generation. We propose a novel technical panorama elucidating RL's multifaceted roles in diffusion-based language, multimodal, robotic, and scientific models, with a granular focus on diffusion trajectory optimization and reward engineering. Through extensive experiments on multiple task-specific benchmarks, we systematically evaluate representative methods to intuitively highlight the advantages of different RL post-training strategies. Furthermore, we reveal and dissect three crucial bottlenecks that currently hinder the real-world deployment of RL-driven DMs: reward design fragility, exploration-exploitation trade-off in high-dimensional generation spaces, and training instability under sparse rewards. Based on these perspectives, we provide a principled roadmap for the integration of RL into DMs and outline promising future research directions for robust, interpretable RL-diffusion systems. We also construct a public repository to continuously track the latest developments in this rapidly evolving field: https://github.com/MAIR-Lab-HUST/Awesome-RL-for-Diffusion-Models.

title: PocketTSLM: Deploying an On-Device Soft-Prompt Time-Series Language Model for Privacy-Preserving Smartphone Reasoning
abstract: Consumer phones and wearables increasingly collect physiological time-series data, yet most mobile systems treat these streams as summaries or text rather than as temporal evidence. This representation is poorly matched to personal health systems that need to retrieve, route, or summarize sensor evidence while preserving temporal structure. Cloud-hosted time-series language models avoid smartphone limits, but they repeatedly move sensitive physiology off the device and add latency and per-query compute cost. Mobile model alternatives that aggregate time-series data into statistical features or serialize raw samples as text either compress temporal structure or exhaust the context and memory budgets of small on-device models. We present PocketTSLM, a mobile-native deployment of OpenTSLM SoftPrompt, the soft-prompt variant of the OpenTSLM time-series language model. PocketTSLM runs fully on a consumer smartphone by injecting encoded time-series windows as embeddings instead of tokenizing time series as text. A numerical parity protocol verifies identical greedy-decoded token sequences between the Swift port and a Python reference using Apple's MLX machine-learning framework. Answers also match the PyTorch reference, although rationale wording can differ. An on-device context-economics benchmark compares the soft-prompt path with a text-serialized baseline on the same backbone. In our benchmark format, soft-prompting uses approximately 12 times fewer time-series tokens and reduces prompt-prefill cost. PocketTSLM processes 30-second Sleep-EDF electroencephalography clips for sleep staging and a 1,000-sample (10 s) 12-lead electrocardiogram clip from ECG-QA. In comparison, text-serialized baselines exceed the phone's context or memory budget at longer time-series windows. All inference runs entirely on the device, with no health data transmitted during inference.

title: OmicsBench: a long-horizon multi-turn benchmark of AI agents on research-study-scale bioinformatics
abstract: Computational biologists increasingly delegate substantial analyses to AI agents in long-horizon, multi-turn sessions, yet most benchmarks of agents' bioinformatics capabilities pose a single short task with a single-shot prompt. We present OmicsBench, a long-horizon, multi-turn bioinformatics benchmark for AI agents. Each of its 97 tasks links dependent subtasks into a directed acyclic graph, for 662 underlying subtasks in all. Each subtask is posed as one user turn and graded deterministically against an answer key, with optional in-context feedback on incorrect answers. Across 12 models on three harnesses, the slowest agent averages 3.6 hours per task, and no combination comes near saturating the benchmark, with mean scores of 0.43 to 0.57 out of a possible 1 without in-context feedback and 0.54 to 0.67 with it. Multi-turn evaluation also uncovers behavior that single-shot prompts cannot, as agents score lower on subtasks that depend on earlier subtasks, and in-context feedback helps agents recover some of that loss. Because deterministic scoring gives no qualitative account of how an agent failed, we also introduce an unsupervised failure mode discovery pipeline that describes, embeds, and clusters agents' failed attempts to surface emergent failure modes. Applied to OmicsBench, this pipeline exposes qualitative shortcomings in how agents carry out bioinformatics analyses, ranging from agents applying their own statistical filters in place of the specified ones to agents writing whole answers from memory.

title: Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing
abstract: Small language models are increasingly deployed on edge devices and robotic systems to meet cost and latency constraints, yet their limited capabilities can make reliable deployment challenging. Stronger models can provide assistance when needed, but deciding when to route a weak-model response to a stronger model often relies on signals of response correctness. In open-ended and agentic tasks, however, obtaining such signals can require costly ground-truth supervision that is difficult to obtain at scale. We revisit the foundations of weak-to-strong routing and ask whether routing decisions can instead be guided by signals that do not require ground-truth supervision. We first characterize the optimal weak-to-strong routing policy, while allowing for multiple weak-model responses generated through local inference. Building on this characterization, we derive a principled approximation to the optimal routing based on model-to-model comparison. In particular, we introduce a notion of model disagreement that can be measured directly from model-generated responses, without ground-truth supervision. Importantly, the approximation becomes increasingly accurate as the strong model becomes a better proxy for the ground-truth distribution. Across agentic and single-turn tasks, our approach effectively navigates the trade-off between routing cost and response accuracy without ground-truth supervision. Moreover, even when ground-truth correctness signals are available for training, disagreement-based routing can outperform methods trained directly to predict correctness

title: Approaching Backpropagation Accuracy with Weight Perturbation on MNIST
abstract: Weight perturbation (WP) estimates learning directions from random parameter perturbations and a scalar change in loss, without backpropagating derivatives. We examine how batch size, training duration, and estimator stabilization affect its attainable accuracy in fully connected MNIST networks. In the shallow configuration, large-batch training reaches approximately 97\% test accuracy, compared with an early backpropagation (BP) reference near 97.5--98\%. The same comparison exposes a substantial efficiency gap: under a ten-epoch budget, shallow WP reaches 90.2\%, whereas the reported BP reference reaches 97.4\%. Epoch-indexed curves show diminishing returns from increasing batch size beyond 4,000. Learning-rate reduction and averaging independent perturbation-based updates also stabilize deeper networks, although their recorded results do not establish BP-level accuracy. We distinguish these empirical findings from a finite-horizon approximation argument: under stated regularity conditions, population WP can approximate a fixed gradient-descent trajectory arbitrarily closely at any fixed finite depth. Positive classification margins then suffice to preserve the reference predictions on a finite test set with arbitrarily high probability. Together, the results identify near-BP accuracy as a configuration- and budget-dependent possibility, rather than evidence of equal efficiency or an unconditional accuracy guarantee across depth.

title: Lethe: Link Inference Attacks For Evaluation of Edge Unlearning Methods
abstract: Graph Unlearning (GU) aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a Graph Neural Network without retraining anew. While most methods address removal of nodes and features, Edge Unlearning (EU), aiming at forgetting edges, has recently attracted dedicated attention as a standalone problem due to the hardness of completely removing the impact of an edge in the model. Despite this, no dedicated benchmark for EU exists besides isolated evaluations on feature-rich datasets such as Cora and Citeseer where GNNs exploit node features rather than graph structure. As such, we show two systematic limitations in existing evaluations: dedicated EU methods can be slower than retraining anew, and accuracy metrics are uninformative due to the negligible impact of edge removal. To address this gap, we introduce Lethe, the first comprehensive benchmark for Edge Unlearning, featuring 15 methods and 8 datasets. Our benchmark emphasizes large graphs, introduces evaluation tasks of varying difficulty, and proposes empirical measures based on link inference attacks rather than proxy accuracy metrics. We provide a comprehensive empirical analysis, demonstrate the shortcomings of current evaluations, and release Lethe as a reproducible, extensible benchmark.

title: Digitalization and Automation in Tourism a Comparative Analysis of Human Tour Guiding and Artificial Intelligence Predictions
abstract: This study examines the professional standing of tourist guides, key actors in the tourism sector, in the context of automation, robotics, and generative artificial intelligence (AI). The empirical framework draws on semi-structured interviews conducted in 2018 with 16 professional tourist guides actively working in Istanbul, alongside responses generated by the ChatGPT-4.1 large language model in 2026 to parallel qualitative research questions. A comparative descriptive analysis reveals both significant convergences and divergences between the two data sources. The findings indicate that 56.25% of human guides and AI agree that automation will quantitatively reduce the need for human guides in routine and information-oriented tours. However, while AI anticipates market segmentation across economic categories, 62.50% of human guides emphasize the human dimension of cultural transmission and do not perceive technology as a direct professional threat. Both sources converge on the view that empathy, emotional connection, humor, flexibility, and storytelling remain difficult to replace through robotic systems. The most notable divergence concerns outdoor guiding: human guides considered it impossible, whereas AI predicted that 5G, GPS, and smart city infrastructures could enable AI-guided outdoor services within 2–5 years. Overall, the study proposes a complementary hybrid service model in which AI assumes operational tasks while human guides focus on cultural interpretation and professional job crafting. It also offers implications for tourism education and digital transformation strategies.

title: Dynamically Bifurcating Tree Networks: A Conceptual Architecture for Growth-and-Pruning–Based Sequence Models
abstract: Most neural sequence models — including the Transformer architectures behind current large language models — use a fixed computation graph: the number of layers, heads, and parameters is set before training and does not change based on what the model encounters. This paper sketches an alternative: a network built from simple recursive units, called neons, that can structurally grow (by splitting) or shrink (by pruning) during operation, so that the shape of the network itself is part of what it learns. A neon accumulates a bounded scalar state; when that state saturates, the unit splits into two child units that inherit the overflow; when a unit's state collapses below a floor, it and its descendants are removed and a record of the removal constrains future growth in that region of the structure. Units at similar structural positions interact multiplicatively, gating each other's state. We describe the mechanism formally, relate each piece to existing, established techniques in neural architecture search, memory-augmented networks, and positional encoding, and lay out the open problems that would need to be resolved before this could be implemented and tested. This is an idea paper: no experiments have been run, and the central claim is that the mechanism is worth prototyping, not that it works. This paper is one of five companion papers making up The Lovial Framework, applying that framework's general concept of relationship-first, recursively stabilizing structure to a concrete AI architecture proposal; here, the role played elsewhere by a Lovial is played by a neon in the process of splitting or being pruned.

title: The invention of a language using existence and two methods of proof through this language
abstract: Causes, causal relationships, and effects can be expressed as a conjunction (logical AND) of statements regarding the existence of certain entities. These existence claims can then be used to construct proofs. There are various methods for such proofs; two of them are presented here. The first method involves converting the converse of a proposition into an existence claim; if expanding this claim leads to the existence of an impossible entity, then the existence claim—and consequently the original proposition—is proven true. The second method is summarized as follows: a proposition based on certain conditions can be reformulated into the form: "If a and b hold, then c is true." Furthermore, the truth value of c is known in advance for each of the three cases: (not a and b), (a and not b), and (not a and not b). When these two conditions are met, a conjunctive statement—formed by combining the assertions regarding the existence of a, b, and c—is established. To identify which existential assertions within this conjunction do not hold, we first determine which ones are valid based on the three aforementioned cases. Next, we translate these existential assertions into alternative expressions and derive further valid existential assertions from those new forms. We refer to the initial set of existential assertions as "first-order expressions" and the subsequent set as "second-order expressions." Within these second-order expressions, it is possible to identify existential assertions that are false. If this process reveals that the statement (a and b ↔ not c) is false, it follows that the statement (a and b ↔ c) must be true.

title: The Economics of Orchestration: Can Culturally-Composed Teams of Small Language Models Outperform Frontier Models at Equal Cost? A Cost-Matched Experiment on Business Solution Generation — Reproducibility Package
abstract: Reproducibility package for the paper 'The Economics of Orchestration'. Organizations deploying large language models face a budget choice: pay for a frontier model, or orchestrate cheaper models into a multi-step pipeline. Across three pre-registered studies (a 2x2x2 factorial over five LLM families and 19 business problems with 1,900 blinded generation-judgment runs, a refinement probe, and an adaptive designer study with a confirmatory replication wave), the paper shows a three-step team structure lifts a lower-tier model to 98.8% of frontier quality at 88% of the cost, while a single lower-tier call captures 98% at 23% of the cost. This archive contains the final paper PDF plus the complete companion repository: all pipeline definitions, prompts, pinned model versions and prices, raw model outputs, token and latency logs, judge prompts and raw scores, analysis scripts, and pre-registration materials — sufficient to reproduce every reported statistic without access to the DeeWaanAI platform used to execute the runs (accessed August–September 2026).

title: DESIGNING AN AI-BASED ONLINE ADAPTIVE LEARNING SYSTEM FOR HIGHER EDUCATION: A CONCEPTUAL MODEL INTEGRATING MULTIDIMENSIONAL LEARNER MODELLING, KNOWLEDGE TRACING AND LMS INTEROPERABILITY
abstract: Universities increasingly rely on learning management systems (LMS) for online and blended learning, yet these platforms rarely adapt instruction to the individual learner. Existing adaptive solutions are often proprietary, isolated from the institutional LMS, opaque to teachers and unavailable for national-language content. Aim. The article presents a conceptual model of an AI-based online adaptive learning system for higher education that integrates a multidimensional learner model, an interpretable adaptation engine and standards-based interoperability with existing LMS. Methods. The study follows the design science research methodology (Peffers et al., 2007). Design requirements were derived from a review of research on adaptive learning, learner modelling and AI in education, and from strategic documents on the digitalisation of higher education in Uzbekistan. The artefact was then designed and specified, and a plan for its demonstration and evaluation was developed. Results. The model comprises five design principles; a domain model structured around knowledge components; a multidimensional learner model combining cognitive (Bayesian knowledge tracing), behavioural and motivational indicators; an adaptation engine that selects learning activities within the learner's zone of proximal development using item response theory; a layered architecture integrated with the LMS via IMS LTI 1.3 and the Experience API (xAPI); and a teacher dashboard that supports human oversight. An evaluation framework with measurable criteria is proposed. Conclusion. The model offers a transparent and technically feasible basis for introducing adaptive learning into national higher education platforms. Its effectiveness will be tested empirically in a quasi-experimental study.

title: Participation Bias Correction for Byzantine-Robust Federated Learning Under Heterogeneous Client Availability
abstract: Federated learning enables distributed clients to collaboratively train a global model without sharing their private data. However, Byzantine robustness becomes more challenging under heterogeneous client availability, since Byzantine clients with higher availability can participate more frequently than honest clients and accumulate disproportionate influence over the global model across rounds. Existing Byzantine-robust aggregation methods mainly defend against malicious updates after the participating clients have been selected, and therefore cannot directly correct the persistent participation bias caused by unequal client availability. This bias can raise the effective Byzantine weight beyond the level assumed by current-round robustness guarantees even when the population-wide Byzantine fraction is moderate. To address this availability-correlated threat, we propose a robust federated aggregation method with participation-bias correction that reduces Byzantine influence based on historical client availability rather than only current-round update information. The key idea of our method is a participation-level correction scheme that controls cross-round client influence before update-level robust aggregation. Specifically, the server first estimates each client’s availability from historical online records and converts the estimates into bounded inverse-propensity weights, assigning smaller aggregation weights to clients that participate more frequently. It then applies temporal difference clipping to limit large deviations from the previously applied server update and aggregates the clipped differences using a weighted geometric median with the corrected participation weights. Extensive experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 under sign-flip and Gaussian attacks demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves robustness when Byzantine clients have higher availability while preserving clean training utility. The results further show that participation bias correction provides the main robustness gain, while temporal difference clipping offers additional stabilization under different availability gaps, Byzantine ratios, and non-IID data distributions while incurring small computation and memory overhead.

title: Enterprise Signature Frameworks and Post Quantum
abstract: Enterprise blockchain deployments demand strong authorization, auditability, and long-term cryptographic assurance. The chapter addresses these requirements by examining advanced signature frameworks designed for organizational and post-quantum settings. Learners will explore identity-based linearly homomorphic signature schemes that enable verifiable data aggregation and fine-grained control without centralized trust. The chapter then analyzes multisignature constructions tailored for enterprise and consortium blockchains, with concrete use cases such as coordinated supply chain approvals. It further introduces lattice-based signature schemes as a practical response to emerging quantum threats. We learn how these schemes achieve quantum resistance and how they compare with classical signatures in terms of efficiency and security.

title: The importance of tensor handling and implementation of physics-informed DeepONets
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) reduce or eliminate the need for large labelled datasets by enforcing governing equations during training. Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks (PI-DeepONets) extend this approach to learning solution operators, enabling rapid prediction across families of problems. Despite these advantages, we show that their application to higher-dimensional problems remains limited by the computational cost of training. To address this issue, we propose a modified PI-DeepONet architecture that reduces this cost by removing redundancy in how the Branch network processes input functions across collocation points. The proposed formulation is mathematically equivalent to the original architecture but reduces input tensor sizes and the number of Branch network evaluations. We analyse the computational complexity of both architectures and derive theoretical scaling laws for training time with respect to the number of collocation points and input functions. The proposed architecture is evaluated on 1D, 2D, and 3D linear advection problems. In all cases, it achieves comparable predictive accuracy to the original PI-DeepONet while consistently reducing training time. In 2D experiments, a maximum speed-up of $3.75\times$ is observed, with empirical training-time scaling agreeing with the predicted linear dependence on collocation points and input functions. Furthermore, training a 3D model on an NVIDIA A100 GPU is only feasible using the proposed architecture, as the original formulation exceeds memory limits. These results demonstrate that careful consideration of how PI-DeepONets are implemented can yield substantial gains, enhancing the practical performance of PI-DeepONets and enabling their application to otherwise intractable physics-informed learning problems.

title: Agent Status Protocol (ASP): A Lightweight Specification for State Reporting in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: The Agent Status Protocol (ASP) defines a lightweight way for heterogeneous AI agents to report their operational state to a status server, and for observers such as dashboards to receive that state as soon as it changes. Agents push small JSON events over HTTP POST; the server exposes the aggregated state to observers over Server-Sent Events (SSE). Because an agent that has crashed, hung or been compromised cannot be trusted to report its own failure, ASP does not rely on self-reports alone: the server infers liveness from missed heartbeats, can detect agents that are alive but no longer making progress, and accepts observations from supervisors, guardrails, operators and peers, some of which take precedence over what the agent says about itself while others are shown alongside it. ASP models state along independent dimensions (lifecycle, health, task, floor, governance), so that an agent can be, for example, online, degraded, working on a task and waiting for the floor at the same time. It reuses existing vocabularies: task states from the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, floor states from the Open Floor Protocol (OFP), and attribute conventions from the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. This paper presents version 0.1 of ASP as a proposal, not as an approved standard. It is a working draft intended to open a discussion, and the authors invite comments, alternative proposals and independent implementations from the community.

Because an agent that has crashed, hung or been compromised cannot be trusted to report its own failure, ASP does not rely on self-reports alone: the server infers liveness from missed heartbeats, can detect agents that are alive but no longer making progress, and accepts observations from supervisors, guardrails, operators and peers, some of which take precedence over what the agent says about itself while others are shown alongside it. ASP models state along independent dimensions (lifecycle, health, task, floor, governance), so that an agent can be, for example, online, degraded, working on a task and waiting for the floor at the same time. It reuses existing vocabularies: task states from the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, floor states from the Open Floor Protocol (OFP), and attribute conventions from the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. This paper presents version 0.1 of ASP as a proposal, not as an approved standard. It is a working draft intended to open a discussion, and the authors invite comments, alternative proposals and independent implementations from the community.

title: Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding and Trusted Rendering for Agent Step-Up Authorization
abstract: AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. We define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting, and run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), the Microsoft action-bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. An audit of ten agent runtimes finds no third-party verifiable approval record, no flood limits where measurable, and post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. As a reference defense we build ASU (Agent Step-Up), a gateway that renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the phone of the user sign its digest, and executes only the stored call. Tamarin proves its binding, single-use and key-level non-repudiation properties under three stated hypotheses (53 lemmas). Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo attack pairs, ASU stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and the trusted card cuts forged-narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03. With 15 current language models as automated approvers, the trusted card raises the attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98, at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses, mostly due to a placeholder artifact in our stimuli. A second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation in these experiments, flooding still succeeds 0.45 to 0.60 of the time against a modeled approver, and approval cannot stop effects that policy already allows. Code, data and proofs: https://github.com/Sports-Vision-Inc/agent-step-up

title: ControlFlow3D: Distilling Multi-View Knowledge into Latent Flow Matching for Point Cloud Upsampling
abstract: Point cloud upsampling is essential for 3D applications but remains challenging due to sparse, under-constrained observations. Multi-view images can resolve geometric ambiguity, but existing multi-modal methods do not fully exploit visual cues. We propose ControlFlow3D, a framework that distills knowledge from pretrained foundation models into a lightweight generation network during training, enabling strong performance without multi-view images available at test time. Specifically, our method performs conditional flow matching in a structured latent space defined by a frozen 3D encoder. Multi-view image tokens and 3D latent tokens are jointly clustered into shared prototypes via unsupervised soft KMeans; the resulting prototypes guide the flow trajectory through velocity control and are aligned by a consistency loss that progressively transfers image knowledge into the base network. A Mamba-based geometry decoder then maps latent features to dense coordinates with linear complexity. We also construct ShapeNetPU, a 35K-object multi-modal benchmark that is 31 times larger than prior datasets. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its strong generalization capability.

title: Local Epochs as Optimal Stopping: Theory and Evidence in Federated Learning
abstract: How long should each client train before communicating? Federated learning usually answers with a fixed, hand-tuned number of local epochs, yet an extra epoch helps only while the loss it removes outweighs the client drift it adds. We cast local training as finite-horizon optimal stopping: a client trains while the next epoch's expected loss reduction exceeds its priced squared drift. We prove that this one-stage look-ahead threshold is optimal whenever stopping decisions are nested, derive closed forms for geometric and power-law returns, and show that an estimated rule loses utility only through wrong-signed decisions. Epoch-level evidence supports the model's structure (geometric diminishing returns and additive drift) and reveals a simple regularity: the stage of training, not the client, sets the budget. The resulting rule, FedStop, is never more than one point below tuned FedAvg in mean accuracy. Where its budgets vary, it raises worst-decile accuracy by 4-8 points over tuned FedAvg and an adaptive-interval baseline, and every one of these gains remains significant after a Holm correction. Against the client-side stopping rules ALT and FLASH, it has the highest CIFAR-10 worst decile on every seed and is level elsewhere. It stays stable where per-client early stopping collapses, and each stopping decision takes constant time.

title: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation consolidates specialist models into one student at the price of rollouts, teacher passes and gradient steps for every teacher. We show that the consolidation does not need training: with forward passes only, the capabilities of separately tuned specialists can be aggregated into one model that is, on average, more accurate than either specialist alone. When specialists share a base model, distillation has an exact layer-wise solution: each linear layer of the fused model must reproduce every specialist's output on the inputs that specialist receives while reading its own answers, a least-squares problem whose solution needs only the second moments of those inputs. One forward pass over a few hundred rollouts provides them. We call this training-free on-policy distillation (\method). What the rollouts contain matters more than the solver: answers truncated in repetition loops are few among a mathematics specialist's rollouts but carry a large share of their tokens, and removing them lifts the fused model on AIME25 from task arithmetic's level to the specialist's at matched precision. On Olmo~3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist yield a generalist that keeps most of each specialist's gain on each of seven mathematics and code benchmarks.

title: OntoAct: Hypothesis-Based Neuro-Symbolic Agents through Ontological Abstraction
abstract: Learning from experience requires recovering reusable knowledge and determining when it applies to a new situation. We introduce OntoAct, a hypothesis-based neuro-symbolic framework built on ontological abstraction. OntoAct turns individual experiences into axioms over entity types, relations, and conditions, making their underlying patterns reusable across situations. A large language model (LLM) uses this world knowledge to propose hypotheses and actions, while a symbolic verifier assesses their supporting conditions against current observations. Verification identifies missing evidence, and new observations and intervention outcomes update hypothesis assessments and guide subsequent actions. We also introduce Tacit-FLE, a benchmark built on the Factorio Learning Environment (FLE) for diagnosing and repairing hidden faults in existing factories using inherited operational records. Its synthetic maintenance corpus distributes evidence across records, and an executed repair may leave the fault unresolved, requiring agents to reassess their diagnoses through interaction. Across Tacit-FLE, Mars, and ALFWorld, OntoAct achieves leading task performance with efficient interaction and inference.

title: Resisting Harmful Instructions through Training-Free Weight Editing
abstract: Instruction-following language models can comply with requests that conflict with intended behaviors and safety alignment. We introduce a training-free weight-editing approach for reducing compliance with targeted undesirable instructions. Our method needs only forward passes on a small set of prompt pairs per target behavior, and because the edit is stored in the model's weights, changing or deleting instructions in the prompt cannot undo the weight modification. We evaluate the approach on two target harmful behaviors across five instruction-tuned models: instructed falsehood and instructed sexism. On two instructed-lying benchmarks, it improves mean honest response rates by 6.2 and 4.6 percentage points over the strongest alternative, significantly on three of the five models and within noise on the other two. In a controlled study of seven prompt formats, it maintains higher honest-response rates than single-layer activation steering when orders to lie arrive in single-turn formats not used to construct the edit. For instructed sexism, it reduces the mean sexist-response rate from 57.9% to 24.3%; combining the edit with a fairness prompt reduces it further to 11.9%. These results establish our contrast-based weight editing approach as an effective training-free intervention in two distinct behavioral domains, supporting its use both independently and alongside prompt-based safeguards.

title: Multi-Reward Hacking: From Aggregation-Induced Drift to Trust-Anchored Defense
abstract: To improve task performance while encouraging desirable response properties, LLM post-training often combines a primary reward (e.g., correctness) with auxiliary rewards (e.g., brevity or efficiency). However, how these rewards are aggregated can critically affect training outcomes. We show that symmetric aggregation, which treats reward channels equally, can induce a failure where aggregate reward improves while primary-task performance degrades, even when individual rewards are meaningful. We investigate this aggregation-induced failure through a one-step multi-reward decision formulation, characterizing when it constitutes multi-reward hacking. We prove that, under symmetric aggregation, deterministic conditional-mean GRPO converges to auxiliary-favoring behavior when auxiliary rewards are more reliably obtained, regardless of initialization. We propose Trust-Anchored Gating (TAG), which first elects an anchor channel based on the policy drift induced by optimizing each channel alone, then gates auxiliary credit on anchor satisfaction. Unlike calibration-sensitive static reweighting, TAG structurally eliminates credit for auxiliary-only outcomes while preserving additional credit for joint success. In the same analytical setting, TAG provably reverses this selection, converging to the primary-favoring action from any initialization when the primary channel is anchored. Experiments across Qwen and Llama models on mathematics and program synthesis reveal substantial degradation under symmetric, constrained, and normalized aggregation, whereas TAG mitigates this failure. On Qwen3-4B with a brevity reward, TAG achieves 0.581 pass@4 versus 0.220 for additive aggregation, while shortening responses by 44% relative to correctness-only training.

title: production-readiness-agentes: marco de preparación para producción de agentes de pre-venta basados en LLM (v1.0.0)
abstract: Marco para decidir si un agente conversacional basado en un modelo de lenguaje está listo para producción, y un caso completo donde se aplica a un agente de pre-venta de ecommerce. Mide tres dimensiones y las consolida en un veredicto conjuntivo: robustez con pass^k, resistencia a la inyección de instrucciones directa e indirecta con la tasa de éxito de ataque, y cumplimiento con un checklist ejecutable derivado de la Ley N° 21.719 de Chile y de la circular SERNAC 2022. Incluye el corpus sintético congelado, las transcripciones de las ejecuciones de cada medición publicada, con las excepciones documentadas en docs/PROCEDENCIA.md, y un verificador que rehace los artefactos derivados sin llamar a la API.

title: Adaptive Self-Reinforcement and Mutual Reinforcement in World Self-and-Mutual Models: A Unified Architecture for Switching Between Independent and Interdependent World-Model Evolution
abstract: World models provide internal representations of environmental states, dynamics, and potential future outcomes. However, improving a world model can follow different learning regimes. A model may improve independently through its own prediction errors, internal consistency checks, counterfactual simulation, and interaction history. Alternatively, multiple world models may improve through mutual evaluation, information exchange, cross-model prediction, and reciprocal correction. Permanently relying on either regime can be suboptimal: independent learning may preserve blind spots, whereas continuous interaction may introduce communication costs, correlated errors, negative transfer, and unnecessary coordination. This paper proposes the World Self-and-Mutual Model framework (WSMM), a conceptual architecture for adaptive switching between self-reinforcement and mutual reinforcement at the world-model level. WSMM is not defined as a large language model, an ensemble of language models, or a conventional multi-agent prompting system. Instead, it is a model-level architecture in which one or more world models maintain internal state-transition representations, evaluate their own predictive performance, and selectively interact with other world models when reciprocal information is expected to improve model quality. title: Geospatial assessment of rooftop solar photovoltaic potential for university campus decarbonization in hot-arid environments
abstract: University campuses in hot-arid environments combine high solar irradiance, large underutilized rooftop areas, and cooling-dominated electricity demand that align closely with peak solar generation. Yet campus-scale assessments in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region remain scarce, and existing studies rarely integrate actual building-level electricity consumption, including parking shade structures as co-equal deployment surfaces, or apply multiregional input–output lifecycle carbon accounting. This study addresses all three gaps through a geospatial assessment of rooftop and parking-lot solar photovoltaic potential at Qatar University, combining high-resolution LiDAR-derived digital surface models with six years of building-level electricity consumption data. Solar radiation modeling in ArcGIS Pro with slope, aspect, and irradiance threshold filtering identified 21 suitable buildings and their associated parking canopy structures. Photovoltaic performance was modeled using temperature-corrected efficiency at 22% for monocrystalline silicon modules, a performance ratio of 0.86, and Qatar-specific climatic parameters. Campus-wide deployment could generate 330,587 kWh annually, split between building rooftops (58%) and parking canopy structures (42%), against a total campus demand of 318,184 kWh, yielding a Campus Self-Sufficiency Ratio of approximately 103.8%. Nine buildings achieve self-sufficiency ratios above 80%, with several reaching net-positive annual energy status. Direct operational CO 2 emissions are avoided, totalling approximately 144.8 tonnes annually. MRIO lifecycle analysis using the EXIOBASE 3 database yields a net carbon footprint reduction of 0.475 kg CO 2 -eq/kWh and a campus-wide lifecycle reduction of approximately 157.0 tonnes CO 2 -eq annually, equivalent to the sequestration of approximately 6,652 mature trees. Eleven high-priority buildings achieve 6 to 7-year payback periods under cost-reflective pricing. These findings provide a replicable framework for institutional decarbonization in hot-arid regions where dust accumulation, temperature-induced efficiency losses, and cooling-driven demand patterns differ fundamentally from temperate contexts.

title: Controlled-Memory Identification with Shared Generators: Dimension--Horizon Tradeoffs and Quantum--Classical Separation
abstract: We determine the finite-horizon identification limits of a \(d\)-dimensional memory when the control interface is restricted to four shared, time-homogeneous generators. A writer encodes a message by applying a prefix word to a common root state. The verifier then applies a candidate-dependent query word followed by a shared terminal binary test, with each word of length at most \(T\). For fixed error tolerances \(λ_2>0\) and \(λ_1+λ_2<1\), the optimal identification sizes satisfy \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d^2,T\})\) for arbitrary CPTP generators and \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d,T\})\) for stochastic maps. Four unitary letters and four permutation letters attain these respective bounds, showing that a four-letter reversible alphabet reaches the static code-size orders in optimal quadratic and linear word length. In the fully dimension-limited regime, this yields \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ(d^2)\) versus \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ(d)\), establishing a quadratic quantum--classical separation in logarithmic code size. Low-overlap Grassmann and agreement-code packings supply the orbit endpoints, while exact inverse query words match each encoded state to its designated test. At the sharp boundary \(λ_2=0\), \(0\leqλ_1<1\), all four model classes satisfy \(\ln N=Θ(\min\{\ln d,T\})\). Thus any fixed positive false-acceptance tolerance activates the metric-packing regime, whereas zero false acceptance imposes an exclusive-witness constraint and yields the logarithmic-dimension boundary.

title: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.

title: VALCON: Benchmarking and Enhancing Value Consistency in Large Language Models via Dual-Role Variation
abstract: Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. Such consistency is increasingly important because modern LLM agents and alignment pipelines often rely on the same LLM to both generate actions and evaluate their acceptability. To mitigate this limitation, we propose VALCON, a role-driven data construction framework that operationalizes value consistency into three benchmark suites (VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, VAB-Challenge) via dual-role variation. By systematically pairing an LLM's generative behavior with its evaluative judgments under identical principles, VALCON synthesizes target evaluation data that exposes hidden value discrepancies. Experiments on 28 LLMs reveal pervasive cross-role inconsistency: models with highly compliant outputs frequently fail to align their judgments with their own generations. To understand and address this gap, we perform mechanistic probing that uncovers a role-dependent representational decoupling associated with this behavioral asymmetry. Guided by these insights, we propose a representation-directed intervention that effectively mitigates consistency failures. Our work establishes value consistency as a distinct alignment dimension and provides a complete evaluation-analysis-mitigation pipeline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/VALCON.
